opus-5.5.text:
I think the most useful way to apply the Bitter Lesson isn't as a blanket dismissal of algorithmic work, but as a lens for asking: does this improvement get better or worse as you add more compute and data? That's really the core of Sutton's point. The methods that won in chess, Go, speech, vision, and language were the ones that leveraged general-purpose search and learning, and could ride the exponential of cheaper compute. The ones that lost were usually clever encodings of human knowledge that gave you a nice bump at small scale and then plateaued or actively got in the way.

So when I look at a new algorithmic idea, the first thing I want to see is a scaling curve, not a single point. If someone says "our method beats the baseline by three percent," my question is: at what scale? If you plot performance against compute, does the gap widen, stay constant, or close? A lot of tricks look great in the small-model regime because they're essentially injecting a prior that the model could have learned on its own given enough data. As you scale up, the baseline learns that prior anyway and the advantage disappears. Those are the improvements I'd be skeptical of.

On the other hand, there's a category of algorithmic improvements that are fully compatible with the Bitter Lesson, and in fact are what make it work. Things like better optimizers, normalization, residual connections, attention itself, mixed-precision training. These aren't encoding domain knowledge about the task. They're making it possible to convert compute into capability more efficiently. If something gives you a constant multiplier on effective compute that holds across scales, that's enormously valuable, because it compounds with everything else. A 2x compute-efficiency gain that persists is basically a free year of hardware progress.

I'd also say there's a subtle trap: researchers sometimes over-apply the Bitter Lesson and conclude that nothing matters except scale. But the history is that someone had to figure out the right architecture and objective that could actually absorb the scale. Transformers didn't invent themselves. Next-token prediction as a universal objective was an insight. So the lesson isn't "don't think," it's "think about the things that let general methods scale, and be humble about the things you think you know about the problem's structure."

In robotics, where I've spent a lot of time, this is especially tricky, because data is so expensive that you're often stuck in the small-data regime where priors genuinely help. The temptation is to build in a lot of structure: hand-designed state representations, kinematic models, task-specific reward shaping. And that works for a demo. But I think the right long-term bet is to ask how to get into the regime where you can collect data at scale, and then prefer methods that will keep improving once you're there. Sometimes the most Bitter-Lesson-compliant algorithmic improvement is actually an improvement to the data engine rather than the model.

So my practical heuristic is: favor methods that remove assumptions rather than add them, demand scaling curves rather than benchmark points, and value anything that makes compute or data more efficiently convertible into general capability.

r001.rationale: The response recommends assessing scaling curves and notes that robotics is currently constrained by expensive data, but it does not frame the judgment as estimating how much scaling can realistically achieve at present.

r002.rationale: It says a persistent compute-efficiency multiplier compounds with other gains; it does not suggest that algorithmic multipliers may fail to compound because their benefits overlap.

r003.rationale: It describes a compute-efficiency advantage that persists across scales. It does not suggest that the advantage diminishes as more powerful hardware becomes available.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the Bitter Lesson is really a statement about what survives scaling, not a claim that algorithms don't matter. Sutton's point was that methods that leverage computation tend to beat methods that leverage human knowledge, and the mistake people make is reading that as "don't do algorithmic work." That's not it. The question is which direction your algorithm points.

So when I look at a paper or an idea, the first thing I ask is: does this improvement get bigger or smaller as you add compute and data? There's a class of tricks that are really about compensating for having too little data or too small a model. Clever inductive biases, hand-designed features, architectural constraints that encode what the researcher believes about the problem. Those tend to look great at the scale they were developed at and then evaporate, or even turn into liabilities, once you go an order of magnitude up. The model would have learned a better version of that prior on its own if you'd just let it.

Then there's the other class, which is things that make the learning process itself more efficient or more stable or more parallelizable. Attention is the canonical one. Attention isn't a "human knowledge" trick, it's a way of letting the model spend compute more flexibly. Same with things like better optimizers, better data pipelines, mixture of experts, techniques that let you use more hardware. Those are algorithmic improvements that are entirely in the spirit of the Bitter Lesson. They multiply compute instead of substituting for it.

The practical heuristic I use is to run the scaling experiment, even if it's small. Three or four model sizes, three or four data sizes. If the gap between your method and the baseline is shrinking as you go up and to the right, you should be honest with yourself that you've probably found a small-scale artifact. If the gap is constant or growing, that's interesting. And the thing people underrate is that a constant gap is still worth a lot. A constant two-x improvement in sample efficiency at every scale is a two-x reduction in cost forever, which at frontier budgets is an enormous amount of money.

The other thing I'd say, especially for people in robotics where I spend most of my time, is that the Bitter Lesson has a timing component. It tells you where things end up, not where they are right now. If you're trying to ship a robot this year, you can't just wait for the data to arrive. So you end up putting in structure that you know is going to get bitter-lessoned eventually, and that's fine as long as you build it in a way that's easy to rip out. The failure mode is when people fall in love with the scaffolding and start defending it after the data has arrived and it's no longer necessary.

So, short version: judge the algorithm by its scaling behavior, not by its benchmark number. Ask whether it's helping the model absorb more compute or helping the researcher avoid needing compute. The first kind compounds. The second kind has a shelf life, and you should know what that shelf life is before you invest a career in it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends measuring how an algorithm performs across model and data scales and notes that Bitter Lesson tradeoffs depend on timing. It does not frame the judgment as estimating how much scaling can realistically achieve at the present time.

r002.rationale: The response says some improvements compound by making compute more useful, but does not suggest their benefits overlap or that this overlap can prevent compounding.

r003.rationale: The response says some tricks lose value as models and data scale, but does not say an algorithm’s computational advantage may diminish as more powerful hardware becomes available.

astra-6.text:
I think the wrong way to read the Bitter Lesson is that algorithms don’t matter and you should just scale up whatever you have. The more useful reading is: look for algorithms that let you benefit from more computation.

An algorithmic improvement can look great at a fixed compute budget because you’ve put a lot of human knowledge into the system. But does that advantage persist as you scale? Or does it impose a ceiling that a more general method eventually blows past? That’s the question I’d ask.

And there’s a distinction between improving performance at one point on a scaling curve and changing how efficiently you can scale. If your algorithm makes learning more parallelizable, or lets you use a much larger source of data, that can be enormously valuable. That’s entirely consistent with the Bitter Lesson.

So I wouldn’t use it to dismiss an algorithmic idea before testing it. I’d use it to choose the experiment: show me what happens across compute budgets, and give me a reason to think this method will keep getting better when we give it substantially more resources.

r001.rationale: The response says to compare performance across compute budgets and assess whether an algorithm keeps improving as substantially more resources are added, which captures judging scaling’s realistic potential.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that compute multipliers fail to compound because their benefits overlap.

r003.rationale: It discusses whether an algorithm’s advantage persists as compute scales, but does not say that the advantage diminishes as more powerful hardware becomes available.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the wrong way to interpret the Bitter Lesson is that algorithms don’t matter and you should just scale up whatever you have. The interesting question is whether an algorithm lets you make better use of more computation.

An improvement can look really good at a fixed compute budget because you’ve baked in some clever assumptions. But does that advantage persist as you scale? Or does a more general method eventually learn the thing you engineered? I’d want to see how the improvement changes the scaling curve, rather than just whether it wins on today’s benchmark.

And there are algorithmic advances that make scaling possible in the first place. Those are very consistent with the Bitter Lesson. So I’d treat it as a research taste heuristic: favor methods that can keep improving with more compute and experience, and be skeptical of ones whose benefits depend on us supplying increasingly elaborate knowledge.

r001.rationale: The response recommends examining scaling curves and whether advantages persist with more compute, but it does not frame the judgment as assessing how much scaling can realistically achieve at the present time.

r002.rationale: It says an engineered advantage may disappear as a general method learns the same capability, but it does not attribute non-compounding compute gains to overlapping benefits.

r003.rationale: It discusses scaling with more compute, but does not say an algorithmic advantage diminishes as more powerful hardware becomes available.
